d.title: From the text of a query to the rows that come back
d.caption: Only the last stage touches data. Everything before it is the engine deciding *how*, from a cost model and a set of statistics that may be days out of date — which is why a query that was fast last month can be slow today with no change to its text.

d.title: Why the planner refuses the index you built
d.caption: A full scan reads pages in order, which is cheap per row; an index scan jumps to a random page per row. Past roughly a few per cent of the table, reading everything in order wins — so an index on a column where 90% of rows match is correctly ignored.

d.title: The four numbers on every plan line
d.caption: EXPLAIN gives you the first two — what the planner believed. EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds the second two — what happened. The distance between `rows=` and `actual rows=` is the diagnosis: when they differ by orders of magnitude, every join choice above that line was made on a false premise.

d.title: What indexes cost on the way in
d.caption: Measured: inserting 50,000 orders takes 54 ms into a bare table, 82 ms with one secondary index and 259 ms with four — five times the cost. Indexes are paid for on every write and repaid only on the reads that use them, which is why `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0` is a column worth checking.

d.title: Counting distinct things, exactly and approximately
d.caption: An exact `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` must remember every key it has seen — a hash of every distinct value, which for a billion events is memory the query does not get. HyperLogLog trades a small, bounded error for constant memory, and for 'roughly how many users' that is the right trade.

d.title: The slowest query is rarely the one to fix
d.caption: Total time is calls times mean time, and that product is what the database actually spends. A 40-second nightly report costs 40 seconds a day; a 30-millisecond lookup running 2,000 times a minute costs an hour a day.
